{
  "permission": {
    "bash": {
      "pip *": "deny",
      "pip3 *": "deny"
    }
  },

    "NEVER use system-wide installed Python packages.",
    "Always create a virtual environment (venv) in the project directory: python -m venv venv",
    "Activate the venv with: source venv/bin/activate (Linux/Mac) or venv\\Scripts\\activate (Windows)",
    "Install packages only within the venv: pip install <package>"
  ]
}
Expected: 
- opencode should block "pip install requests" and ask for approval
- opencode should create a venv (python -m venv venv) instead of using system pip with --break-system-packages
Actual:
- Command runs (blocked by PEP 668 by the system) but no permission prompt shown
- opencode debug config shows the permission is loaded correctly, but it's not enforced
- The instructions are ignored - model still tries to use system pip
This makes it impossible to securely use opencode with Python projects.

hit this exact three-way split wiring a local PTT dictation loop for a desktop agent last quarter. the shutdown hook gap is the sneakiest. std::process::exit(0) to kill a dangling hotkey thread works until the transcription worker has a half-flushed audio buffer and you corrupt the next session's first utterance. the fix that held up was giving the hotkey listener a crossbeam channel and a select! loop so a parent shutdown token cancels it cleanly, but that only works if the host actually fires a shutdown event.

on the inject vs send question, I'd push back on the framing. users want both and the right split isn't policy, it's length. anything under ~4 words is a command and should send; longer utterances should stage in the input so you can fix the inevitable whisper mis-hears of proper nouns. we ended up with a config flag plus a hard cap because the "always stage" mode felt clunky for short confirmations.
